extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially those learning dialogue mechanics) and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using dialogue tags, action beats, and punctuation conventions for fiction dialogue in US English; explains what counts as tags vs. beats and how to punctuate and format dialogue lines and interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of dialogue tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue tags (or speech tags) indicate who is speaking and how the dialogue is being said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tags should be actions that a character can perform with the speech they’re producing. Common dialogue tags: said, asked, exclaimed, shouted, muttered, whispered, yelled, mumbled, hissed. The purpose is to tell the reader who’s speaking; keep focus on what’s being said rather than on the tag itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'said' as neutral tag
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Said' is by far the most common dialogue tag and is often effectively invisible to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some advise avoiding repeated 'said', many readers treat it as neutral. Avoid over-creative variety in tags because it can distract. Instead of adding adverbs (e.g., 'she said excitedly'), prefer 'said' or a stronger verb; "less can be more."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overusing adverbs with tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers often add adverbs to describe how something is said (like excitedly or quickly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again, less can be more; use a stronger dialogue tag or an action beat rather than piling on adverbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversy over 'hissed'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'hissed' can be a controversial dialogue tag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some readers insist you can only 'hiss' sibilant sounds (e.g., 'Shush!'), while others accept 'hissed' for any angry whisper. There aren't many single-word alternatives that convey the same sentiment, so it’s a stylistic choice—'do you.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Spoke' is not a dialogue tag
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'spoke' (past tense of 'speak') is generally not considered a dialogue tag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where 'said' refers to what’s communicated, 'spoke' refers to the act of communicating itself (e.g., 'She spoke in German'). It does not indicate how the line is said and so is not a proper tag for marking dialogue lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of action beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Action beats show what a character is doing before, during, or after their dialogue; these can be gestures, movements, or facial expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a strict sense, these acts cannot be done to the speech itself. Examples: smiled, sighed, shrugged, gestured, nodded. There is disagreement about mouth actions (gasped, breathed, laughed) — some editors object to them as tags though they appear in published fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation mark convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks are used around all lines of dialogue (US English).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post states: 'Quotation marks always go outside the punctuation, regardless of whether it’s a period, comma, exclamation point, or question mark.' (Note: this is the original wording from the post; follow the post's stated convention or your house style.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing dialogue by speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Each speaker gets their own paragraph for their dialogue, whether it’s one line or multiple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps readers follow the conversation because the new paragraph distinguishes a new speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation of dialogue tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue tags are punctuated with commas and double quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the tag follows the dialogue, the first word of the tag is lowercase (unless it’s a proper noun). Examples: '“I’d like that,” she said.' and 'She said, “I’d like that.”' Also: "I’d like," she said, "that piece..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation of action beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Action beats are punctuated with periods or other terminal punctuation (exclamation/question marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The punctuation goes inside the quotation marks for the dialogue. The action beat is its own sentence and should be capitalized (e.g., 'She smiled. “I’d like that piece of chocolate cake.”').

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining dialogue tags and action beats
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining a dialogue tag with an action, the element closest to the dialogue determines punctuation (comma vs. period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '“I’d like that piece of chocolate cake,” she said, smiling.' 'She smiled and said, “I’d like that piece of chocolate cake.”' '“I’d like that piece of chocolate cake.” She smiled as she said it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes within dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: If something is being quoted within a line of dialogue, use single quotation marks around the quoted part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '“What did you mean by ‘that piece of chocolate cake’?”'

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrupted speech (em dash)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that is cut off or self-interrupted is indicated with an em dash (—).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When speech is self-interrupted and restarted, a space after the em dash can be used but is optional. Examples: '“I—I’d like that piece of—”' and '“I don’t— Actually, I would like that piece of chocolate cake.”' (the post notes the optional space after the em dash.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Trailing speech (ellipsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that is faltering or trailing off is indicated with an ellipsis (… or . . .).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no space between the ellipsis and the closing quotation mark. Examples: '“I’d like . . . that piece of chocolate cake.”' or '“I’d like that piece of chocolate cake . . .”'

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech interrupted by an action — punctuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A line of dialogue can be interrupted by a dialogue tag or by an action beat, and punctuation differs accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If interrupted by a dialogue tag, use commas to set off the dialogue before and after the tag: '“I’d like that piece,” she said, pointing...' If interrupted by an action beat, use em dashes outside the quotation marks with no other punctuation next to the interrupting action: '“I’d like that piece”—she pointed toward the table—“of chocolate cake.”'

rubrics_metrics.name: Uninterrupted dialogue over multiple paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character has a long speech broken into multiple paragraphs, use an opening quotation mark at the start of every paragraph but a closing quotation mark only on the final paragraph, provided there are no intervening non-dialogue bits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This signals that the same person continues speaking across paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of dialogue and tags/beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue moves the story forward and provides insight into characters’ thoughts and feelings; tags and action beats ground the dialogue in the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fiction writers, being able to punctuate dialogue is an essential skill (or one an editor can help with). Use tags and beats to show what’s being done and how things are being said, always privileging clarity and story movement.
